Heating 
Heating pipework to be generally run in either Steel tube to BS3601, table X copper or stainless 
steel with pipes dropping to radiators in copper. Drops to be concealed within cavity of walls where 
possible with no joints behind walls. 
Press-fit systems are only to be used on copper or stainless-steel pipework. The use of carbon 
steel cannot be used due to corrosion and issues raised in Estates & Facilities Alert EFA/2016/001. 
No heating pipework shall be exposed; all pipes within rooms to be insulated and concealed or 
boxed in. 
 
Radiators to be LST Deep Clean, sloping top, wall mounted type (such as Contour LST with 
internal TRV kit 9210-13). TRV temperature to be set at 20⁰c. Where radiators are not LST, they 
shall have LST casings supplied and installed by Contour Casings Ltd.   
 
All valves to be Hattersley except TRV’s. 
 
 
Domestic Water Services 
All Hot Water Services shall be run in copper tube (table X), with thermostatic mixing valves or 
TMV 3 mixer tap used at each required outlet point. They shall be in accordance with HTM 04-01 & 
ACOP L8. 
 
Hot and Cold Water Pipework to be concealed wherever possible or chrome plated wherever on 
show. Clinical Wash Hand Basins to use I.P.S. arrangements, to enable a concealed trap and 
waste. All concealed pipework to be insulated to NHS standards. Isolating / double reg valves to be 
Hattersley. Quarter turn lever operated ball valves shall be provided to enable individual isolation of 
each outlet / mixing valve in lieu of Balofix valves. All fitting to WRAS approved. No flexible hoses 
shall be used.

Ventilation 
Ventilation to comply with HTM 03-01 and CIBSE guides. Ductwork installation shall comply with 
DW144. Consideration shall be given to specified ventilation exchange rates following Covid-19 to 
reduce transmission rates and reduce times between any Aerosol Generated Procedure’s (AGP’s) 
Access doors shall be fitted in accessible locations as per DW144 to allow maintenance/inspection 
of fire dampers, volume control dampers, mesh screens, etc. 
Fire dampers to be Swegon Actionaire smoke dampers wired back to an existing or new Actionpac 
LNS 5 damper panel. Dampers to generally be mode 6 operation. Installation to comply with 
DW145 
The Mechanical Contractor’s ductwork specialist shall supply and install suitable access panels to 
each damper in accordance with DW144 and DW145 & the Actionair Approved Fire & Smoke 
Damper Installation Manual. Access doors shall be fitted adjacent to each smoke damper to 
enable visual inspection of the damper blades from the same location as the damper actuator and 
test switch – i.e. installation must facilitate a 1-man ‘damper test operation’. 
 
External Fire Hydrant 
There is a fire hydrant rind around the perimeter of the site. As part of the fire strategy, it shall be 
calculated whether additional fire hydrant outlets are required. Where required it shall meet the 
requirements of BS9990. 
 
Internal Dry Riser 
As part of the fire strategy, it shall be determined whether a dry riser is to be provided. Where 
required it shall meet the requirements of BS9990.

by Autometers Ltd. 
Boards / Panels to be labelled with traffolite label.

Fire Alarm. 
Fire alarms shall conform to BS 5839 and HTM 05-03B with L1 coverage. 
The site has an existing Static Systems Ltd, Advanced MXPro5 networked addressable fire 
detection system. Detectors shall be Apollo discovery range. Allow for all new Apollo loops in the 
panel, allowing for 20% spare capacity. 
Sounders shall be Viper VPR-MT direct wired conventional sounders wired from local Panel. There 
shall be a sounder circuit for each zone in the building. Sounders shall not be wired from the loop. 
Wiring shall meet enhanced standard and be fire rated pliable cable with red low smoke and fume 
sheath. Wiring shall be concealed in all areas except in plantrooms where it may run surface in 
trunking. 
All software information shall be agreed with the trust prior to sending to Static Systems. Software 
will be required for Panel, the site data station, and central controller.

Voids and difficult to access areas shall employ the use of and Aspirating system. The system shall

system. 
 
Nurse Call 
The nurse call system shall comply with HTM 08-03 Bedhead Services. The system shall be the 
Static Systems Ultima full IP system. The system shall be connected to the hospital data networks 
to allow remote interrogation from maintenance staff. 
Commissioning to by Static Systems and be witnessed by the Trust. 
 
Communications. 
All data and phones shall be wired over a structured cable network to a central cabinet or hub 
located in a dedicated comms room. Wiring shall meet category 6a standard and be coloured ice 
blue. Outlets to be RJ45 type labelled with the cabinet and port number. Ensure there are sufficient 
outlets in each room for all PC’s, printers, phones etc with a minimum of one spare outlet per room. 
Data shall be wired back to the main hospital server room located on the ground floor Trust 
computer room and to the Main Theatres Comms room. Wiring to be 50/125 8-core multimode 
OM4 fibre optic with 8 port patch panels at each end with LC terminations. Allow for mounting Trust 
issued Cisco switches in the cabinet. Provide patch panels sized for the number of outlets. Allow 
for provision of 16 no fibre patch leads. Allow copper patch leads, of suitable lengths to patch 
between the patch panels and switches, quantity to be 75% of number of outlets. 
Provide a multi core telephone cable from the Trust main telephone switch to the cabinet 
terminated onto a voice patch rail.  Wirral Installations Ltd currently undertake the Trust telephone 
wiring and commissioning. 
The Trust shall appoint cisco to undertake a full Wi-Fi coverage survey. Allow for mounting the 
Trust supplied Cisco WiFi Access points onto the ceilings and patching in.

Our Approach to Design Management 
We are a highly experienced and trusted ALDT that builds on personal relationships established over 
several years on the successful delivery of many projects.  We combine global best practice, NHP 
programme expertise and project specific local knowledge. 
 
As lead designer, Ryder Architecture bring experience of managing large design teams to 
successfully deliver complex projects in healthcare and other sectors, meeting the demands of 
challenging programmes across project stages.  For Whipps Cross Hospital, Ryder led the ALDT to 
deliver an OBC-ready design together with a successful hybrid planning application within nine 
months of appointment.  This was achieved in the context of an evolving clinical brief and schedule of 
accommodation, and alongside a complex programme of external stakeholder engagement that 
included multiple local authorities and statutory consultees.  We are similarly leading the design team 
for West Suffolk Hospital and led the ALDT for the National Rehabilitation Centre for Nottingham 
University Hospitals before being novated to the successful contractor. 
  
Underpinning our success on these projects was a commitment to effective communication within 
a clear project structure, set out for all in our Project Execution Plan (PEP).  The PEP is a live 
Quality Management System (QMS) that provides control of project deliverables and assurance of 
quality, programme and cost. 
 
Integral to the successful delivery of the PEP will be a regular Principals’ Forum – a forum to ensure 
the strategic direction of the whole project.  Given the pace of the OBC phase we propose this forum 
meets fortnightly to look ahead and plan, bringing together the design principals, cost manager, PM 
and key client team.  
  
Working Collaboratively and Managing Cost 
We will generate a one team ethos from the outset, collaborating to make the complex simple, 
working for the project rather than our constituent parts, to provide creative certainty, proactive 
leadership, trusted design processes and continuous learning.  This is critical to develop the project 
brief, test this iteratively with the Hospital 2.0 reference design and meet the programme demands.  
We will build on our knowledge from the SOC stages to drive ownership of project deliverables and 
ensure we work to a common goal from the outline masterplan strategy to the digital infrastructure.  
Regular “drum beats” will ensure all disciplines are pulling together, in time, as one.  
  
Our international innovation and knowledge will challenge and inform whilst maintaining your ‘Good 
Customer’ approach towards NHP and delivering your Healthier Future vision  for all of your 
communities and users.  We will work with you to deliver a model hospital that is efficient in its 
planning and workflow to support sustainable whole life costs, with flexibility to adapt to pace of 
change within a core physical and digital infrastructure that is accommodated within your initial capital 
budget.  
  
Design sprints are our principal method of progressing a single, unified solution and will be planned 
to include MCHFT’s Project Delivery Group and Estates Redevelopment Programme Board.  We will 
engage across the workstreams of your project delivery structure to deliver an OBC that meets your 
vision of an Adaptable, Sustainable, Innovative, Efficient and Safe healthier future.  Sprints help forge 
a greater team spirit and improved communication with the entire team, including NHP stakeholders, 
working as one.  We have demonstrated this approach in our work with you on the SOC development, 
working proactively to engage with the NHP team to interpret and integrate emerging Hospital 2.0 
principles into an arrangement that will establish Leighton as the Hospital 2.0 low rise reference 
project.  
  
We will proactively manage costs – identifying and addressing potential issues early, providing 
appropriate advice to inform the design process and ensure delivery within budget.  We have been 
proactive in engaging with your cost consultants throughout the SOC stages.  Moving into OBC, the 
ALDT will work alongside the cost consultant to take collective responsibility for the cost plan and 
contribute to the management of the balance between cost, programme and quality.  Our design 
sprint methodology ensures high quality design, detail and specification developed 
collaboratively with cost planning factored into all of our decision making at this critical stage . 
We recognise a robust and complete OBC will allow the successful introduction of the main 
contractor, reducing delivery risk and enhancing overall cost certainty.

Managing Additional Strategies 
Our innovation in the use of digital design technology includes parametric design tools, energy 
analysis and sequencing analysis, providing significant added value in design efficiency, project risk, 
energy efficiency, material usage, the intelligent operation of buildings and buildability.  Our  
information management specialists will establish an agreed digital protocol that will form the basis of 
coordinating the inputs of all specialists into a digital twin for Leighton. 
 
Our ALDT teams contain FM, healthcare planning and digital infrastructure experts.   We will manage 
their inputs at the right times to avoid surprises or design derailment.  We will add value from 
lessons from a diverse range of other international projects, exemplified in developing BIM for FM 
interfaces for Sydney Opera House and work for BMW across their global facilities. 
  
Managing Additional Consultants 
Fundamental to the success of integrated design is a one team ethos commitment from every 
member to embrace the required behaviours set out in our Project Charter.  The Charter requires all 
to agree to act in good faith, in an open, trusting and cooperative manner, avoiding disputes by 
adopting a ‘no blame’ culture, valuing the skills, respecting the responsibilities of each other in an 
environment where we can all challenge.  We work in a common digital environment which improves 
knowledge sharing, improves communication, improves stakeholder understanding, analyses 
workflow and space optimisation and to ensure effective coordination.  
  
We will provide clarity of leadership ensuring the input and coordination of all design consultants, 
maintaining a strategic overview of the project, anticipating and guiding the team through challenges 
and opportunities. 
  
Hospital 2.0 Compliance 
We have worked hard to develop positive relationships with the NHP team and a good understanding 
of the evolving Hospital 2.0. We are continuing to progress this through our ongoing wider NHP work 
in addition to our SOC stage work at Leighton.  Respecting project confidentiality, we will facilitate 
effective lessons learned across our NHP projects for the benefit of Leighton and the wider 
programme.  Our recent work at West Suffolk to develop the design in line with Hospital 2.0 concepts 
has gained excellent NHP feedback. 
  
We will fully embrace the benefits of Hospital 2.0 of delivering quicker, with greater control and 
assurance, whilst reducing cost and carbon. 
 
 
 
Our Commitments to Leighton

• Avoiding ambiguities through clear, candid communication and jargon free, simple 
explanations to ensure common understanding  
• Embracing appropriate and agreed technologies  
• Supporting each other in the training and the development of our people  
• Being innovative and open minded, prepared to explore and experiment, testing ideas 
robustly and at the right time  
• Taking professional pride in a collective ambition, leaving our professional silos behind  
• Respecting deadlines with the timely delivery of information and services  
• Engaging early and take collective responsibility to create coordinated, well considered, 
simple, elegant solutions  
• Recording relevant decisions and providing transparency and certainty of information

data environment and facilitating timely decision making.

movements on site, reducing emissions and disruption.  This approach will significantly reduce the 
impact of construction on the operation of the existing estate.

1 We are aware that significant engagement has already taken place and we bring the benefit of

Lessons from previous engagements: 
  
1 Consistency of stakeholders at workshops is critical.  In developing the OBC for the redevelopment

the new service.

Obtaining an Optimum Solution 
In addition to the stakeholders and groups already engaged we will seek to include those who so far 
may have not been involved.  This could include community engagement to extend the reach of public 
consultation especially with those who are typically underrepresented and who do not tend to engage 
through traditional methods, such as those in the region’s more socially deprived communities, 
younger generations, busy parents, those with disabilities and minority groups.  
 
Consensus building is essential.  We take an open and honest approach to dealing with issues, we 
are not afraid to confront difficulties as we recognise projects benefit from a better understanding of 
the constraints and decision making process.  
  
One of the first steps to obtaining an optimum solution will be stakeholder mapping to compile a list of 
all potential stakeholders before categorising them.  An effective stakeholder map will ensure every 
party is listened to, and the design responds to needs that have been carefully and accurately 
analysed.  It ensures the right people provide input to the most appropriate aspects of the project, and 
others are kept informed to encourage co ownership and enthusiasm. It allows us to channel 
disparate, and perhaps conflicting requirements, through the filter of the briefing blueprint objectives. 
These objectives – your non negotiables – provide the foundation on which to build, interrogate and 
incorporate the nuanced feedback from a wide range of stakeholders effectively and efficiently.  
  
Infection Prevention and Control 
Our clinical specialists will engage with your IPC lead team to ensure the design not only complies 
with current legislation but actively considers thought leadership around future best practice bringing 
lessons from the ALDT’s project experience and our wider knowledge. Some examples of recent 
detail considerations include: 
• Incorporating an ultra-green route into day surgery so that planned and un-planned clinical 
teams and patients can be permanently segregated from each other in the event of any future 
pandemic or similar infectious outbreak 
• Incorporating permanent dividing partitions within surgical admission and discharge bays in lieu 
of cubicle curtains to reduce infection risks to patients that had just undergone surgery  
• Designing an endoscopy clinical flow to not only achieve JAG guidance, but also segregate 
patients to ensure a single direction of flow, improving the control of infection.  
 
NHP Coordination 
We will support the Trust with its ongoing discussions with the New Hospital Programme across its 
Transformation, Delivery and Commercial workstreams whilst ensuring compliance to all relevant 
legislation, policies and guidance;  
  
We envisage the Leighton ALDT, MCHFT and NHP H2.0 teams working as one throughout the 
development of the OBC solution and submission of planning.  One of the first tasks for the leadership 
team on inception / kick off, will be to develop a communication plan, drum beat of key meetings and 
reviews and an integrated team zipper.  This will enable each team to have a recognised 
“accountable” individual, and clear and obvious communication route to manage and implement the 
NHP H2.0 processes and design standards in the most seamless manner, informing Technical 
Reviews and gateway approval.

Supporting Buildability 
The Building Safety Act (BSA) demands a digital golden thread of data throughout the life of the 
new Leighton Hospital. This ‘golden thread’ will run through the design, construction planning and 
operational phases.  We bring significant experience in delivery of Stage 2 BIM, aligned to BS EN 
19650, embedding geometric and non-geometric data to enhance our design delivery. 
  
We will bring a digital first approach using our combined modelling to embed non-graphical data to 
inform sequencing of delivery (4D) and capture Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) directly from the 
model (5D+).  
  
Our smart modelling approach will include logistics and phasing parameters, material 
specifications, CDM risks, durability, and Level of Information Need (LOIN).  This will be supported by 
visualisations to give clear unambiguous guidance to contractors. 
  
Our automated systems can not only be used to extract material quantities for continual cost 
monitoring, we bring further added value by collating upfront embodied carbon metrics to support 
the completion of the NHS Net Zero Building Standard (NZBS) toolkits.

We have a thorough vetting process that we apply when we are required to appoint 
subconsultants. As a matter of course our subconsultants are financially vetted, their PI cover 
checked and basic competencies interrogated through a suite of questionnaires that require 
completion before we appoint.

entering / accepting a subconsultant agreement is that it is entered into on a back to back basis 
with our main appointment with the client.  We make the main appointment available to the 
subconsultant for inspection and review to ensure they are fully aware of our duties and 
obligations under the main appointment.  
 
Our supply chain’s competency is subject to review on a project by project basis which is then fed 
into the bi monthly leadership forum which has a standing agenda item for partner performance. 
Any issues are taken up by the project directors with the subconsultant.  This is also reviewed on 
an annual basis to ensure continued competency.  
 
We regularly feedback to our key subconsultants on their performance and have resolution 
ladders where senior members of both organisations can speak more frankly than at project team 
level and if required request improvements or personnel changes.

Table 1. Outline of timeframes and the owner of each social value commitment  
 
Objective 1: Skills, employment and workforce equality and inclusion 
1. No. of weeks of training opportunities on the contract  
 
Target and Baseline: 52 weeks of training opportunities. 
 
Methodology: We will utilise our pioneering and award winning PlanBEE apprenticeship programme. We can 
allocate and support one student based in the projects affiliated office on a rotational basis. This opportunity 
enables them to enhance skills and receive training while actively contributing to project advancement. The t raining 
will contribute evidence towards successful attainment of a Level 4 HNC and Level 5 HND qualification, upon 
completion of the programme. 
 
Evidence: The PlanBEE programme boasts a total of 74 graduates and over 500 placements completed to date. 
99% of graduates have progressed to permanent positions or full honours degrees, with 100% pass rate on the 
End-Point Assessment in 2021, 2022, and 2023. 
 
2. No. of weeks spent on meaningful work placements or pre-employment course 
 
Target and Baseline: 20 weeks of meaningful work placements.   
 
Methodology: The team is dedicated to creating stronger ties with local schools and educational institutions. We 
will leverage our partnership with Cronton Sixth Form College, a member of the Design, Engineer, Construct! 
(DEC) schools programme established by Class Of Your Own (COYO). We will collaborate with Cheshire and 
Warrington Pledge Partnership and their Careers Hub to offer structured, full time work placements for one to two 
weeks. 
 
Evidence: We engaged in the COYO 2023 design competition, inviting students worldwide to conceptualise a Net 
Zero Neonatal Unit for the future in collaboration with the NHP. This extended to guiding students at Buxton School 
through the design process of a net zero neonatal unit, harnessing modern construction techniques and the 
importance of sustainable materials and energy solutions.  
 
3. No. of hours of 'support into work' assistance provided to unemployed people through career 
mentoring 
 
Target and Baseline: 3 x two-hour workshops delivered to 15 attendees.  
 
Methodology:  We will raise awareness of the wide range of STEM careers available among school, college and 
university students, adults not in employment, education, or training (NEET) and those returning to the sector or 
looking for a career change, including members of the armed forces community.  We will leverage our Finding your 
Future programme and partnerships with COYO, the Armed Forces Career Transition Partnership and Launchpad, 
to offer interactive activities such as mock interviews, CV clinics and urban design competitions alongside digital 
learning modules and webinars that increase industry exposure and build career readiness.  
 
Our digital learning resources can be provided as downloadable guides, workbooks and recordings made available 
to participants beyond contract end and provided to MCHFT.  
 
Evidence:  We currently deliver training and skills development support to a Launchpad residence at Speke House 
in Liverpool, Avondale House in Newcastle, and Hollyacre House in Durham.  Launchpad assists veterans to

processes, as well as strategies and interventions to meet sustainability objectives that  can enable and enhance 
operations for this work and for future projects you deliver.

generate tailored recommendations and action plans for Trusts on how they can improve their performance in this 
area going forward.  Our experts also hosted a webinar on ‘Biodiversity Net Gain for the Health Sector’ that was

Methodology: We will draw on our existing partnerships with local charities and initiatives such as OnSide Crewe

fundraising, delivering community outreach and support services, targeting young people, those who are battling 
homelessness and deprivation, and serving personnel, veterans and families in need.  Collaborating with these 
partners we will identify opportunities that align with their missions and deliver the most value. We can also 
promote mental health awareness and mental first aid among their staff, partnering with organisations like Mates in 
Mind to deliver tailored training and awareness sessions. 
 
Evidence: In celebration of Ryder's 70th anniversary, we set out on an ambitious mission to raise £70,000 for local 
charities and community projects.  Through a combination of volunteering time and fundraising initiatives, we 
generated an equivalent of £177,849 and since extended our support to 20 pro-bono projects,  demonstrating our 
dedication through an additional contribution of £70,702 in terms of time and resources.  
 
7. No. of hours volunteering time provided to support local community projects  
 
Target and Baseline: 150 hours of staff volunteering.   
 
Methodology: Utilising our existing relationships with local environmental charities and partners, we will build new 
local partnerships with organisations such as Bring Wildlife Back and Groundwork Grozone, to promote 
environmental conservation.  Our Champions will organise two events on a quarterly basis, five volunteers per 
session, encouraging project staff engagement and working through any risk assessments. We will include 
volunteering activity and identify further volunteering opportunities for this project.  
Evidence: Our social value experts working on NHP are developing a volunteering bank, set to launch in May 
2024.  It will capture volunteering time across NHP staff and supplier networks, track supported community 
initiatives and, log suggested activities to generate greater social value benefits, aligned to hospital Trust 
outcomes. This will assist hospital Trusts with improving and expanding volunteering initiatives to achieve lasting 
social impact.   
1197 / 2000 words

Declaration of Resource Dedication and Consistency 
Project Title: 
Provision of Architect Lead Design Team (ALDT) Services for the New Leighton Hospital 
Client: 
Mid Cheshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (“Trust”) 
Bidder Name: 
Ryder Architecture 
Date: 
5 April 2024 
1. Introduction
This declaration is made to outline the commitment of Ryder Architecture in providing 
consistent and dedicated resources for the Provision of Architect Lead Design Team (ALDT) 
Services for the New Leighton Hospital to the Trust. 
2. Resource Consistency
Ryder Architecture hereby declares that the team members and resources allocated to the 
Provision of Architect Lead Design Team (ALDT) Services for the New Leighton Hospital will 
remain consistent throughout the project lifecycle. Any changes in team composition or key 
resources will be communicated to the Trust project coordinator with immediate effect and will 
be subject to approval by the Trust. 
4. Continuity Assurance
In the event of unforeseen circumstances leading to the departure of key team members or 
resources, Ryder Architecture commits to promptly providing equivalent or superior 
replacements to ensure project continuity and to meet the agreed timelines and quality 
standards. 
5. Compliance and Reporting
Ryder Architecture will regularly update the Trust on the status of resources and project 
progress. Any deviation from the agreed resource plan will be reported and discussed with the 
Trust to find an amicable solution. 
6. Acknowledgement and Agreement
By signing this declaration, Ryder Architecture commits to upholding the terms outlined herein, 
ensuring that the resources intended for the Trust will remain constant, barring unforeseen 
circumstances where replacements, if necessary, will be of equivalent or superior capacity.

Paul Bell

Health and Safety Policy 
 
 
 
 
Project number 
Date 
Author 
Checked by 
 
 
02010:37 
8 August 2023 
Mark Thompson 
Stewart McKenna 
 
 
 
1.0 Purpose and Scope 
 
1.1 Ryder Architecture Ltd is committed to achieving and maintaining high standards of health and 
safety in relation to our people and in respect of visitors to our premises, contractors working 
within our property, and any other persons who may be affected by our activities.  We are aware of 
and committed to meeting our duties under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 and 
associated legislation, in particular the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015.   
 
1.2 
 
The purpose of this policy is to: 
• Prevent accidents and cases of work related ill health 
• Manage health and safety risks in our workplace 
• Provide clear instructions and information, and adequate training, to ensure all our colleagues 
are competent to do their work 
• Provide personal protective equipment as required 
• Consult with our employees on matters affecting their health and safety 
• Provide and maintain safe equipment 
• Ensure the safe handling and use of substances 
• Maintain safe and healthy working conditions 
• Implement emergency procedures, including evacuation in case of fire or other significant 
incident 
• Review and revise this policy on an annual basis 
 
2.0  Responsibility 
 
2.1 
 
The responsibilities within the organisation and the arrangements for implementing the policy are 
set out as below. 
 
2.2 The managing partner takes ultimate responsibility for this policy. 
 
2.3 The quality director is responsible for maintaining and implementing this policy. 
 
2.4 To ensure health and safety standards are maintained / improved, the following people have 
responsibility in the following areas: 
• Safety director – risk assessments, accident and incident investigation 
• Ryder360 chair – work related health (including mental health), consulting employees, 
information instruction, monitoring and training 
• Client service coordinator – emergency procedures, fire evacuation, maintaining equipment 
and first aid 
 
2.5 All colleagues should: 
• Cooperate with supervisors and managers on health and safety matters 
• Take reasonable care of their own health and safety; and report all health and safety concerns 
to an appropriate person (as detailed above)

3.0 Procedure 
 
3.1  Risk assessment 
 
3.1.1 We will complete a risk assessment of the company’s core functions and services on an annual 
basis.  These risk assessments will be reviewed and signed by all colleagues to confirm that the 
information is understood. 
 
3.1.2 We will assess the requirement to review these risk assessments if working conditions change 
significantly during the year. 
 
3.1.3 Individual risk assessments will be carried out for any work outside of our core business activities 
that pose a significant risk. 
 
3.2 Training 
 
3.2.1 All colleagues will receive a general health and safety induction when they join Ryder. 
 
3.2.2 All colleagues will receive an office induction for their place of work. 
 
3.2.3 All colleagues will adhere to manual handling objects around the office guidance. 
 
3.2.4 All colleagues will receive display screen equipment assessment training on an annual basis. 
 
3.2.5 All technical colleagues will receive asbestos awareness training on a bi annual basis and will be 
supported in obtaining a relevant CSCS card to facilitate site visits. 
 
3.2.6 No persons will be allowed to attend a construction site without a CSCS card. 
 
3.2.7 We will provide personal protective equipment to all colleagues as required by our risk 
assessments. 
 
3.2.8 We will make sure that suitable arrangements are in place for employees who work remotely. 
 
3.3 Consultation 
 
3.3.1 We will consult colleagues routinely on matters relating to health and safety as they arise and 
formally when we review our health and safety policy and procedures. 
 
3.4 Evaluation 
 
3.4.1 We will make sure that escape routes are well signed and kept clear at all times. 
 
3.4.2 Evacuation plans for each office will be tested at least every six months. 
 
 
 
Mark Thompson 
Managing Partner

Instructions
General;
1.1 The purpose of this procurement exercise is to appoint a Architect Led Design Team Services to provide services covering RIBA Stages 2 to 3. Bidders are to note that the appointment is 
through to completion of the Outline Business Case which is currently targeted as July 2025.
 
1.2 The project is currently concluding RIBA Stage 1 and is due to commence RIBA Stage 2 in June 2024. Bidders are expected to commence services from 31st May 2024 as set out in the 
tender timetable (2.2).
 
1.3 The Authority reserves the right to extend the contract for the Architect Led Design Team Services beyond RIBA stage 3 (including Outline Business Case delivery) without the need for a 
further procurement exercise. In exercising its discretion to extend, the Authority will consider the successful bidder’s performance up to the point it is considering any extension and whether any 
benefit to the overall programme to extending with the current supplier outweighs any potential benefit in carrying out a further procurement exercise.
 
1.4 Bidders are to note that the design may reach a fully complete RIBA stage 3 by the end of the Outline Business Case and therefore fees are to be on the basis of this.
For Commercial Schedule:
2.1 The Trust requires pricing to be submitted using the template, as follows:
2.2a Fixed price (exclusive of VAT) for the delivery of Architect Led Design Team Services as outlined within the MCHFT Specification (Annex B1) for RIBA Stages 2 & 3.
2.2b The Trust reserves the right to extend the contract to cover additional RIBA stages as required. For information only please provide the requested information for RIBA Stages 4 and onwards.
2.3 The price must be submitted for the total cost of ownership.
For Resource Schedule:
3.1 The Trust requires a full and complete response using the template, to outline all staff members proposed to deliver the services outlined in the MCHFT Specification (Annex B1) for RIBA 
Stages 2 & 3.
3.2 References are only required for Key Person 1.
3.3 Pease add additional lines where required to fully complete your response.

Scope Context
The ALDT shall include the below specialist services:
Core Architectural Services, Lead Design Coordinator and the below architectural specialisms:
•  Clinical Design
•  Experience with standardised design programmes
•  Digital Architect
•  Daylight/Sunlight
•  Wind
•  Landscaping (including Biodiversity Net Gain)
•  Catering
•  Waste and Logistics
•  Lighting
•  Acoustics
•  Inclusive Design
•  Façade Access
•  Façade Engineering
•  Urban Design 
•  Responsible Design (Carbon, Biodiversity, Social value, etc)
•  BIM Support (Use of; ISO19650, Standard AIR and EIR’s, Standard MIDP’s & TIDP’s)
Core Mechanical, Electrical and Plumbing (MEP) Engineering Services and the below specialisms:
•  Digital infrastructure 
•  Core and biodiversity net gain
•  BREEAM
•  Net Zero Carbon (Embodied and Operational)
•  IT and AV
•  Lifts
•  Security
•  Fire Engineering
Core Civil and Structural (C&S) Engineering Services and the below specialism:
•  Transport Planning
Please note that Principal Designer, Healthcare Planning and Medical Equipment Specialist services are to be provided by others and not by the Architect Lead Design Team.

staff working spaces with the external

1 Introduction / Purpose 
This policy sets out the standards that staff within Mid Cheshire Hospitals NHS 
Foundation Trust  (MCHFT) MUST adhere to in relation to confidentiality and data 
protection.  
 
The Trust has a legal obl igation to comply with all appropriate legislation in respect of 
the privacy laws of the Un ited Kingdom. It also has a duty to comply with guidance 
issued by the Department of Health  and Socia l Care  (DHSC), NHS Digital, NHS 
England, the Information Commiss ions Office (ICO) and other advisory groups to the 
NHS. 
 
Patients and staff  entrust us to process their sensitive information relating to  their 
health care, treatment and employment. They do so with the confidence that the Trust 
will keep this information safe, and that staff will use it appropriately. Failure to do this 
carries significant risks to patient safety and has the potential to undermine public trust 
in the NHS . Failure to comply with this policy also puts not only the Trust at risk of 
regulatory enforcement but individual staff may be held accountable if they have acted 
outside of the law.  
 
The purpose of this policy is to ensure that no staff brea ch thei r lega l duty of 
confidence, allow others to do so, or attempt to breach any of the Trust’s s ecurity 
systems. The term ‘staff’ is used to refer to all those whom this policy should apply  
including Trust staff, contractors, volunteers, students, locums and agency staff.  
 
It is the policy of the Trust that no one will be discriminated against on grounds of age, 
disability, gender reassignme nt, mar riage and civil partnership, pregnancy and 
maternity, race, religi on or belief, sex or sex ual orientation . The Trust will provide 
interpretation services or do cumentation in ot her mediums as requested and 
necessary to ensure natural justice and equality of access. 
 
2 Scope 
This policy applies to the processing of all personal information by Trust contractors, 
volunteers, students, locums and agency staff. 
 
The policy applies to all personal information held or processed by the Trust including 
that related to patients, staff, contractors, vis itors, members and third-parties. Where 
specific rules apply to certain types of information, for example patient information, this 
is made clear in the policy. 
 
Whilst th e requirements of t his policy are tailored to personal information it is 
recommended that staff also exten d its content to the proces sing of other types of 
sensitive information, for example sensitive security information. 
 
3 Confidentiality and Data Protection 
In the United Kingdom confidentiality and data protection obligations are conveyed by 
a series of interconnected laws, regulations and statutory guidance. These include but 
are not limited to: 
 
1. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) 
2. The Data Protection Act 2018  
3. The Human Rights Act 1998  
4. The Department of Health and Social Care - National Data Guardian 
Standards  
5. The Security of Network & Information Systems Regulations (NIS 
Regulations)  
 
Docusign Envelope ID: E1235339-C0B7-4B11-A6C0-59B2F210CBB7

=== PDF PAGE 332 ===
 
Confidentiality and Data Protection Policy v7.0 
Page 5 of 39 
The GDPR sets out seven key principles (the data protection principles) which lie at 
the heart of the UK data protection regime. These are: 
 
1. Lawfulness, fairness and transpar ency – information MUST only be 
processed (used, shared, retained) where it is fair and lawful to do so. 
Patients and staff MUST be aware how their data is being processed.  
2. Purpose limitation – information w ill only be used for the purposes it was 
collected or a related purpose where it is necessary to do so.   
3. Data minimisation – only process the minimum amount of data needed to 
achieve your objective. 
4. Accuracy – all reasonable efforts MUST be made to ensure data is accurate.  
5. Storage limitation – information MUST only be retained for as long as is 
necessary. 
6. Integrity and confidentiality – information MUST be kept secure. 
7. Accountability – there MUST be appropriate records and measures in place to 
demonstrate compliance with these principles and the GDPR. 
 
In addition to these principles staff MUST also follow the Caldicott principles: 
 
(1) Justify the purpose(s) of using confidential information 
(2) Use confidential information only when it is necessary 
(3) Use the minimum necessary confidential information 
(4) Access to confidential information should be on a strict need-to-know basis 
(5) Everyone with access to confidential information should be aware of their 
responsibilities  
(6) Comply with the law  
(7) The duty to share information for individual care is as important as the duty  to 
protect patient confidentiality  
(8) Inform patients and service users about how their confidential information is 
used 
 
Whilst these principles a re largely similar the data protection principles special 
emphasis must be drawn to the seventh principle in that staff MUST be aware that the 
duty to share information for individual care is as important as the duty to protect 
patient confidentiality. 
 
The policy outlines the key compliance standards all staff MUST demonstrate when 
processing the personal data of patients, staff or third parties.    
 
Due to the complex natures of some of these requirements the Trust has specific 
policies and procedures surrounding so me of the m. These should be read in 
conjunction with this policy and include: 
 
• Freedom of Informat ion Act and Environment al Information 
Regulations Policy 
• Corporate Records Management Policy 
• Social Media Policy 
• Information Risk and Management Policy

• Data Security and Protection Incident Reporting Procedure 
• Data Protection Risk and Assurance Procedure 
• National Data Opt-Out SOP

3.1               Transparency and Fair Processing 
Personal information MUST be processed in a fair and transparent manner 
with data subjects informed about how their data will be used. The Trust 
primarily fulfils this obligation by including both a patient and staff privacy 
notice on its website. These notices MUST be continually reviewed to ensure 
it remains up to date. Whilst these notices are managed by the Information 
Governance Team, all staff are responsible for ensuring that they reflect any 
new processing activities. These notices can be provided in an alternative 
format by contacting the Information Governance Team. In addition to this, 
individual specialities and those service areas undertaking new or innovative 
ways of using personal data may have their own privacy notice to ensure that 
processing remains transparent.  
 
Privacy notices can be communicated by a variety of means including orally 
or through signs however will, in the main, be communicated on the Trust’s 
website.  
 
Privacy notices will often take a layered approach to avoid information 
overload, duplication and confusion. For example, as part of its transparency 
obligations, the Trust MUST communicate the contact details of its Data 
Protection Officer. This is included on the Trust’s General Privacy Notice 
located on its website, as such it is not generally necessary to communicate 
this in every departmental specific privacy notice.  
 
The Trust MUST ensure that the following information is communicated to 
data subjects regarding all processing of personal data: 
 
• The identity and contact details of the Data Controller and Data 
Protection Officer.  
• Information regarding the lawful basis for processing data. This 
includes details of any sharing of the information.  
• The categories of personal data being processed and whether this will 
be transferred outside of the UK. 
• The period in which the personal data will be retained for. 
• The existence of data subject rights, including how to complain to the 
Information Commissioners Office, and guidance on how these can 
be exercised.  
• The existence of automated decision-making including profiling.  
 
3.2         Lawful Basis and Consent  
The Trust MUST only process personal information where there is a lawful 
basis to do so. 
 
The lawful basis for processing patient information will usually be because it 
is necessary as part of the Trusts ‘publish task’ as an NHS provider for the 
purpose of patient care and treatment. However, where this is not an 
alternative, lawful basis must be identified before personal is processed.  
 
The lawful basis for processing staff information will usually be because it is 
necessary as part of their ‘contract’ of employment. However, where this is 
Docusign Envelope ID: E1235339-C0B7-4B11-A6C0-59B2F210CBB7

=== PDF PAGE 334 ===
 
Confidentiality and Data Protection Policy v7.0 
Page 7 of 39 
not the case, an alternative lawful basis must be identified before personal 
data is processed. 
 
Another key lawful basis is where the processing of personal data is required 
by law. This could include sharing information with the Courts or the 
regulating body such as the NMC. 
 
If the processing of personal data is not necessary as part of another legal 
basis the Trust will need the data subjects’ consent before data is processed.  
 
There are several other key lawful basis which can be used to legally process 
personal data. These are referenced in Appendix 1. However, if staff 
questions in this area, especially when developing new process involving 
patient or staff personal data, they should contact the Trusts Information 
Governance team for advice.  
 
3.2.1 Consent  
It is important to note that the GDPR/Data Protection definition and use of 
consent is different to that of patient consent to treatment.   
 
The GDPR/Data Protection definition of consent is where consent is being 
relied upon as the lawful basis to process personal information. Although 
patients will be asked for their consent to treatment, the lawful basis for 
processing their personal data in this way is because if forms part of the 
Trusts ‘public task’ as described above.  
 
If it is necessary to process personal data outside of any other lawful basis 
(see Appendix 1) then consent must be obtained.   
 
If consent is required it must be: 
• Prominent and not obscured within a larger document 
• Not assumed, including a positive opt-in (no pre ticked boxes) 
• Use clear, plain language that is easy to understand 
• Specify how data will be used 
• Specify why the data needed and what it will be used for 
• Explain how data subjects can withdraw consent if they wish 
• Record how and when consent was provided 
• Regularly review the consent to ensure that is still valid  
 
It is recommended that consent is provided in a written format where possible 
to ensure that an assurance record can be maintained. An example consent 
form is included in Appendix 2. Staff are permitted to gain verbal consent 
however this MUST adhere to the above standards.  
 
3.3 Communicating Personal Information  
There are multiple ways in which personal information can be communicated. 
It is important that staff select the most appropriate method of communication 
when communicating personal information and that they have due regards to 
the data protection principles. Guidance on specific areas of communication 
has been provided below.  
 
3.3.1 Communicating by Text Messages 
Text messages can provide an effective way to communicating personal 
information. However, consideration MUST be given to the potential 
confidentiality risks before communicating in this way.

When planning  to use tex t mes saging, services need to conside r 
carefully issues rega rding confidentiality and clarity of message s. 
Services should take into account that the message may be received by 
someone other than the intended recipient, for example if a mobile phone 
is used by more than one person.  
 
When considering sending text messages staff MUST ensure that: 
• The message does not include personal identifiers such as name, 
date of birth, address or NHS/Staff Numbers. 
• The mess age must only include  the minimum information 
required to achieve its purpose. For example, it is accept able to 
issue patient with a scan appointment reminder however it would 
not usually be necessary to provider details of the part of the 
body being scanned or the reason for the scan.  
• All reasonable efforts MUST be made to ensure that the message 
is sen t to the  correct mobile number. This i s likely to include 
checking Trust records to ensure that the most up to date mobile 
number is being used.  
 
3.3.2 Communicating by Telephone 
When communicating by telephone it is important to remember people’s 
right to expect that their personal information will remain confidential. It is 
essential therefore, to verify that  you are speaking to the correct person 
(see the Verifying Identity section of this policy).  
 
Patient confidential in formation MUST never b e given out to other 
members of the household  without the patient ’s consent . If someone 
other than the patient answers the phone: 
• State your name and that yo u are calling from the Hospital (Staff 
should not confirm their area of work if doing so would result in the 
sharing of sensitive or medical information about the patient) 
• Do not leave a message  which could revea l any confid ential 
information unless it is vital to mitigate an urgent risk to the 
patients’ health. 
• Offer to ring back at a more convenient time, 
 
3.3.3 Contacting Patients by Video Conferencing Media such as Teams  
It will often be necessary to con duct patient meetings and consultations 
using virtual platforms such as Microsoft Teams. When using virtual 
solutions, the following MUST be considered: 
 
• Consider whether this is the most appropriate way of 
communicating with the patient. Consider whether a telephone or 
face to face meeting would be more effective  
• Ensure the patient is able to use the virtual facility 
• Only record the meeting if necessary and ensure that the patient 
is fully aware and consents to the recording taking place  
• If you are conducting the meeting whilst you are working from 
home ensure it cannot be overheard by others in your household  
 
Please n ote that staff MUST onl y use  methods of video conferencing  
approved by the Trus t Information Technology or In formation 
Governance team.

Face to face meetings and consultations with patients wi ll often be the 
most appropriate form of communication. However, it is important to

3.3.5 Communicating via Email 
Patients or service users can request that the Trust correspond with 
them via email providing the service area manging their care can 
accommodate this within their local processes.  
 
The Trust is responsible for the safe transmission of data to patients as 
such this must be sent in line with the secure email standards of this 
policy (see the E-mailing Confidential Information section). 
 
The Trust cannot however guarantee the security of data once it reaches 
the patient. Patients MUST be advised of this before personal 
information is shared with them via email.  
 
In order to ensure that information is sent to the correct email address it 
is recommended information is sent in response to a patient’s initial 
email.  
 
Ensure the correct use of the BCC function. An example of this could be 
where staff are operating an HIV support group. Including recipients 
email addresses in the ‘CC’ or ‘TO’ fields could reveal their identity as 
such the ‘BCC’ function MUST be used in these scenarios.  
 
Do not include personal or confidential information in the subject line. 
 
Please note - patients requesting access to their medical records 
MUST be directed to the Legal Service department for this to be 
considered under the Subject Access process (see Access to 
Records Policy for further details).  
 
Please note that emailing patient information to partner originations 
is dealt with in Information Sharing of this policy. 
 
3.3.6 Communicating via Post 
Corresponding via post remains one of the safest and most reliable ways 
of communication with patients and staff. However, staff MUST take all 
reasonable steps to ensure that correspondence is exchanged safely, 
securely and in line with this policy. Staff MUST always: 
 
• Check that letters are address correctly 
• Check letters are going to the subject’s most recent address 
• Avoid handwriting addresses where possible 
• Mark letters that contain sensitive or personal information as 
‘Private and Confidential’ 
• If the content of the letter is  especially sensitive, consider using 
Recorded/Special Delivery or a tracked courier service 
 
All personal i nformation/data MUST be addressed  to a person, a post 
holder, a consultant or a legitimate safe haven, but not to a department, a 
unit or an organisation. The use of acronyms is not acceptable. In cases 
where the mail is for a team it sh ould be a ddressed to an agreed  post 
holder or team leader. 
 
Information posted to patients should be enveloped a nd addressed in an 
appropriate and secure manner. Information other than the patients name

3.3.7 Communicating with Relatives and Patient Passwords 
Patient information MUST only be shared with their relatives when the 
patient has given their consent for this to be done.  
 
Patient passwords can often facilitate a safe and confidential mechanism 
to communicate information about a patient to their relatives such as 
those who are unable to visit or live out of area. 
 
Passwords MUST be agreed with patients. Once the password has been 
agreed it should be made clear that it is the responsibility of the patient or 
carer to ensure that this password is not shared with others. The 
passwords can be used by other family members; however, the Trust 
accepts no responsibility for unauthorised sharing of passwords by 
patients or relatives.  
 
3.3.8 Recording Patient Meetings and Consultations 
Trust staff MUST only record patient meetings and consultations where: 
• It is necessary to do so 
• The patient has given their consent for the recording to take place 
and that consent has been manged in line with the consent 
section of this policy 
• The recording is made in an open and transparent way 
• Due regard has been taken of the data protection principles 
outlined with this policy  
 
Please note – patients are at liberty to make their own recording of 
meetings and consultations. Further information in this area is 
provided within the Trusts Photography/Images Policy. 
 
3.3.9 Verifying Identity  
Staff MUST ensure that they have verified the identity of recipients prior 
to disclosing personal or sensitive information.  
 
There are several recommendations on how this can be achieved: 
• Asking for identification such as a copy of a driving licence or 
passport  
• If you are talking to a patient or member of staff ask them to 
confirm at least three unique details about themselves i.e. 
address, date of birth and last appointment date 
• If the call has video facilities (webcam), you are able to see the 
caller and are confident they are the right person (ie you have met 
them before) it may not be necessary to ask them to confirm these 
details  
 
This is not a complete list and staff should use their judgement as to 
whether they are assured as to the identity of the individual. If there is 
any doubt as to the identity of the person, staff MUST not share any 
personal or sensitive information.

3.4 Maintaining Information Accuracy 
Staff MUST take all reasonable steps to ensure that personal information is 
accurate.  
 
It is good practice for patients and staff members to be regularly asked if their 
details have changed so they can be updated on Trust systems.  
 
Data subjects should be reminded that if their data is being processed by 
more than one area of the Trust, they should ensure changes are reported to 
all relevant areas. For example, a member of staff may notify their change of 
address to HR however this will not necessarily update their patient records 
held by the Trust. 
 
It is however important to note that whilst the Trust will do everything it can to 
ensure that the personal data it holds is up to date it is ultimately the 
responsibility of the data subject to report these changes.  
 
3.5 Anonymisation and Pseudonymization 
Anonymisation of per sonal data  is the process of removing personally 
identifiable features from data  sets so that th e perso n can no longer be 
identified directly or indirectly. 
 
Anonymised data is not within the scope of the GDPR however care must be 
taken to ensure that the data subject cannot be indirectly identified. For 
example, describing a patient by  their age, e thnicity, gender , condition  and 
admission date would be likely to indirectly identity them. 
 
Pseudonymization is a data  management and de-identification procedure by 
which personally identifiable information fie lds within a data  record are 
replaced by one or more artificial identifiers, or pseudonyms. 
 
Pseudonymized data is in sc ope of the G DPR and the requirements of this 
policy MUST be followed when processing it.  
 
See the Trusts Anonymisation and Pseudonymisa tion Procedure for further 
information in this area.  
  
3.6 Integrity and Confidentiality 
Maintaining the confidentiality and integrity of the personal information held 
by the Trust is vitally important. Failure to do this could not only result in harm 
to patients and staff but also reputational damage of the Trust and NHS and 
regularity action including significant fines.  
 
This section breaks down the key components in maintaining the integrity and 
confidentiality of data held by the Trust. 
 
3.6.1 On Site Security 
 
3.6.1.1 Office Working 
Offices at the Trust can range from dedicated office areas only 
accessible to staff, to banks of PC’s on wards partially accessible 
to patients.  
    
 In all instances precautions must be taken to ensure that personal 
data is not accessible to unauthorised persons. This will include:

3.6.1.2 Records Storage 
When not in use, physical records containing personal

with access limited to authorised staff only 
• A locked cabinet   
• Confidential information MUST be locked away in secure 
storage areas when not in use and not left on desks  
• Desks MUST be kept clear in order to ensure that the 
risk of data loss is minimised 
 
Personal information stored electronically should be stored on 
the Trust’s network servers or Cloud storage, not stored on local 
hard drives. This will ideally be a structured filing system such as

3.6.6 Data Protection Risk and Assurance 
The Trust has a statutory obligation to remain accountable for ensuring 
that appropriate measures are in place to assess and where necessary 
mitigate against data protection risks. This is primarily achieved by way of 
the following mechanisms.  
 
3.6.6.1 Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) 
A DPIA is a ‘l iving’ process to help manage and review the privacy 
risks of the processing of personal data  and the measure s put in 
place to reduce those risks. 
 
The completion of the DPIA is a statutory requirement in many 
instances and as such it is the Trust’s policy that the undertaking of 
a DPI A will be c onsidered at the outset of all new processes, 
services, systems or initiatives, that are introduced or changed, that 
utilise patient or staff persona l data  in order to ensure  that 
implementation of that process does not re sult in an adverse 
impact on the individual’s privacy rights. 
 
Project leads are responsible for the co mpletion of DPIA’s however 
advice MUST be sort f rom the Information Governance Te am 
before risks are accepted.  
 
An Information Asset and Flow Mapp ing Assessment MUST also 
be completed for every new process involving the use of personal 
data.   
 
Further in formation i s a vailable in the Data  Protection Risk and 
Assurance Procedure. 
 
3.6.6.2 Data Processors  
The Trust is generally regarded as a ‘Data Controller’ is respect of 
Data Protection la w meaning that is responsible for and make s 
decisions on how personal data will be used.  
 
However, the Trust also utilises other organisations and companies 
to undertake work on its behalf. When the und ertaking of this work 
involves the use of p ersonal dat a the third-party organisation is 
considered to be a ‘Data Processor’. 
 
The Trust has a statutory obligation to ensure that it has a contract 
in place with all Data  Processors which fulfils the requireme nts of 
the G DPR (s pecifically Article 28) . This contract is som etimes 
included within the Trusts standard contract templates however the 
Trust also ha ve a standalone template available (Data Processing 
Agreement). 
 
All suppliers MUST also provide adequate assurances of their 
compliance with the GDPR. 
 
Project leads are responsible for ensuring that all data processors 
have the appropriate data processing contract in place an d that 
they have provided adequate assurance. These MUST be reviewed 
by the Information Governance Team before data is s hared with 
suppliers.

3.7 Online Meetings 
The use of online meeting services within the NHS is now commonplace and 
there exists an opportunity to realise significant benefits and shift the channel 
by which consultations  can take place. It is however vitall y important to 
consider the confidentiality implications for using an online meeting to discuss 
personal information.  
 
  The Trusts preferred tool for only meetings is Microsoft Teams. This should 
be the default mechanism that staff use for online meetings. The use of other 
tools such as WebEx is  permitted, however, these must not be used to 
communicate personal or sensitive information. Staff must not attempt to 
download desktop versions of these applications without first speaking to the 
IT Help Desk.  
 
When undertaking sensitive online meetings that involve the communication 
of sensitive or personal data, staff MUST ensure they are working in an area 
where conversations cannot be overheard, and that the computer screen 
cannot be observed.  
 
Meetings involving Tru st staff or staff from partner or ganisations may be 
recorded. It is recommended that staff are informed that the meeting will be 
recorded before the record ing starts. Any staff that join the meeting la te will 
be aware that the meeting is being recorded by the presence of the recording 
banner. Recording meetings with patients MUST be done with the consent of 
the patient. All staff are reminded that the recording may be later disclosable 
under the provisions of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. 
 
Staff should not use video/teleconferencing to discuss matters that may 
cause a patient distress or anxiety, or to discuss matters of particular 
sensitivity (eg informing a patient that they have been diagnosed with a 
terminal illness or potentially distressing diagnosis).

3.8 Sharing Confidential or Personal Information 
The sharing of personal information MUST always be done in line with the law 
and Trust polices.  
 
This section only applies to the sharing  of personal information. The sharing 
of anonymised information is not within the scope of this section.  
 
The data protection principles MUST be followed in all instances of the 
sharing of personal information. These are described below with particular 
reference to how they apply to information sharing.  
 
1. Lawfulness, fairness and transparency – there MUST be a lawf ul 
basis to share personal information. The lawful ba sis is defined 
within the GDPR and are referenced in Appendix 1 of this policy.  
Information sharing must be done fairly and transparently, and data 
subjects MUST be aware that their information is being shared (see 
Transparency and Fair Processing of this policy).  
2. Purpose limitation – information sharing MUST be proportionate to 
the purpose in which it is being requested. It must not be used for 
any other purpose unless legally required to do so. The purposes 
for which information is being shared must be validated with the 
requesting organisation if unclear.  
3. Data minimisation – only share the minimum amount of information 
required to achieve the aims of the request.  
4. Accuracy – all reasonable attempts MUST be made t o ensure the 
accuracy of information being shared. I f the information is 
potentially inaccurate the recipient organisation must be informed 
about this.   
5. Storage limitation – information MUST only be retained for as long 
as is necessary. 
6. Integrity and confidentiality – information MUST be sh ared 
securely. Staff must verify that they are sending  the information to 
the correct recipient via secure means (see the Communicating 
Personal Information section of this policy).  
7. Accountability – in all instances there MUST be a record made of 
what information is being shared, why it is being shared, when, who 
by and with whom . This record should be  recorded within 
structured filing sys tem such as the patient’s medical records  or 
staff personal file.  
 
The decision to share personal information will often come down to a decision 
as to whether the risks of not sharing information outweighs the risks o f not 
doing so.  
 
When considering thi s staff MUST keep in mind the seventh Caldicott 
Principle in that duty to share information for individual care is as important as 
the duty to protect patient confidentiality.

3.8.1 Sharing Information for Healthcare Purposes  
NHS Trusts process patient information as part of their public task as an 
NHS provider for the purposes of administering patient care and 
treatment.  
 
Patient information can be shared with other healthcare providers 
however a lawful basis must be identified.  
 
Patients should be asked for consent to their information being shared as 
part of their care and treatment plan. Consent is not however the lawful 
basis to process data in this way (see the consent section of this policy). 
 
3.8.2 Sharing Information for Social Care Purposes 
Information can be shared with social care providers for the provision of 
their public task for the provision of social care services. 
 
Information can also be shared where it is required for the purpose of 
safeguarding children or individuals at risk.  
 
3.8.3 Sharing Information for Clinical Auditing Purposes 
Information will usually only be shared for this purpose where it is: 
 
• Required by law 
• With the patient or staff member’s consent 
• Where the Confidentiality Advisory Group (CAG) grants the 
use of confidential patient information without consent under 
the following regulations of Control of Patient Information 
Regulations 2002, Section 251 of the NHS Act 20065. 
 
3.8.4 Sharing Information with Parents and Carers 
Young people aged 16 or 17 are presumed to be competent for the 
purposes of consent to treatment and are therefore entitled to the same 
duty of confidence as adults. Children under 16 who have the capacity 
and understanding to take decisions about their own treatment are also 
entitled to decide whether personal information may be passed on and 
generally to have their confidence respected.  The key issue here is the 
‘competence’ of the child. If the child is competent then their consent is 
required to disclose and use information.  
 
Carers often provide valuable healthcare and, subject to complying with 
the requirements outlined in this policy, every effort should be made to 
support and facilitate their work. Only information essential to a patient’s 
 
5 Staff must have due regards the National Data Opt-Out section of this policy in this instance.

3.8.5 Sharing Information with Hospital Chaplains 
Spiritual care cannot often be practicably provided without access to 
some confidential patient information and this form of care is strongly 
desired by a proportion of patients. However, the explicit consent of 
patients is required before confidential information is disclosed to 
chaplains. 
 
Where a patient is not competent to consent to disclosure, eg due to 
unconsciousness, the decision rests with those responsible for the 
provision of care acting in the best interests of the patient. The views of 
family members about what the patient would have wanted should be 
given considerable weight in these circumstances. 
 
3.8.6 Sharing Information with Members of Parliament 
Information may be shared with a Members of Parliament if confirmation 
is received from them to confirm that: 
• The patient or member of staff has given their consent for the 
information to be shared 
• They are acting on behalf of the patient or staff member as part of 
their public office as Members of Parliament 
 
3.8.7 Sharing Information with Government Departments 
The requesting department must highlight a lawful basis for the sharing 
of information as part of their request.  
 
The most likely lawful basis for sharing information with government 
departments is that it is required by law. However, this requirement must 
be clear before information is shared.  
 
3.8.8 Sharing Information with Regulatory Services such as the Nursing 
and Midwifery Council (NMC) or Information Commissions Office 
(ICO) 
Regulators will often have statutory provisions to require organisation to 
disclose information under certain circumstances. Where these 
provisions are in doubt staff MUST ask the requester to confirm what 
their lawful basis is for requesting the information.  
 
3.8.9 Sharing Information with the Police and Other Law Enforcement 
Agencies 
Whilst the police have no general right of access to health records there 
are a number of statutes which require disclosure to them and some that 
permit disclosure. 
 
The Trust has created specific guidance to support staff in consideration 
of this area which is included in this policy as Appendix 3. 
 
3.8.10 Sharing Information with the Courts Including Coroner’s Court, 
Tribunals and Enquiries 
The courts, some tribunals and persons appointed to hold enquiries have 
legal powers to require disclosure of confidential patient information. 
 
Care needs to be taken to limit disclosure strictly in terms of the relevant 
order, the precise information requested to the specified bodies and no

3.8.11 Sharing Information with Solicitors 
Most information requests from solicitors for medical records for 
compensation claims are considered under the Subject Access Request 
process (SAR) (see the following section). 
 
Information may also be shared with the Trust Solicitors where they are 
acting on behalf of the Trust.  
 
Requests from solicitors should be directed to the Legal Services Team.  
 
3.8.12 Patients or Staff Accessing their Own Information (Subject Access 
Request (SAR)) 
Data subjects have a right of access to their own personal information 
subject to exemptions. 
 
Requests under this process should be forwarded to the Legal Services 
Department for management in line with the Access to Records Policy. 
 
3.8.13 Sharing Information with the Media 
Requests from the media will usually be managed by the Trusts 
Communications Team. Staff MUST not disclose information directly to 
the media unless authorised to do so.  
 
Under normal circumstances there is no basis for disclosure of 
confidential and identifiable information to the media. There will be 
occasions however when NHS organisations and staff are asked for 
information about individual patients. Examples include: 
 
• Requests for updates on the condition of particular patients, eg 
celebrities 
• In distressing circumstances, eg following a fire or road traffic 
accident 
• In circumstances where a patient or a patient’s relatives are 
complaining publicly about the treatment and care provided 
 
Where practicable, the explicit consent of the individual concerned 
should be sought prior to disclosing any information about their care 
and treatment, including their presence in a hospital or other institution.  
 
Where consent cannot be obtained or is withheld, disclosure may still 
be justified in the "exceptional" public interest. 
 
In distressing circumstances, care should be taken to avoid Breaching 
the confidentiality of patients whilst dealing sympathetically with 
requests for information. Where a patient is not competent to make a 
decision about disclosure, the views of family members should be 
sought and decisions made in the patient’s best interests. 
 
Where information is already in the public domain, placed there by 
individuals or by other agencies such as the police, consent is not 
required.

3.8.14 Sharing Information with Suppliers 
Patient information can be shared with the suppliers of health care 
services where they are processing that data to fulfil a service on the 
Trusts behalf. 
 
Staff must however ensure that there is suitable contractual assurances 
in place before any information is shared in this way. Further information 
in this area is contained within the Data Protection Risk and Assurance 
section of this policy.  
 
3.8.15 Disclosing Personal Information as part of Freedom of Information / 
Environmental Information Requests 
Disclosures of personal information are ordinarily prohibited under 
Freedom of Information legislation.  
 
In some cases, however, personal inform ation may b e released under 
the Freed om of Information Act 2000 or Environmental I nformation 
Regulations 2004. Decisions about di sclosure in these c ases MUST be 
made by the Information Governance Team. 
 
Further information on Freedom of Information / Environmental 
Information Requests  can be found within the Trus ts Freedom of 
Information Policy. 
 
 
3.8.16 Disclosing Personal Information as part of The Civil Contingencies 
Act 2004 
The Civil Contingencies Act 2004 identifies the Trust as a Category 1 
responder. As such, it places a duty on the Trust to share information 
with responding agencies, to assist and cooperate in responding to an 
incident. This includes patient data and personal sensitive data where it 
is required to assist the incident response (such as a major road traffic 
incident or a terrorist attack). In these circumstances, the default position 
is to share as a way of saving lives and preventing harm. 
 
However, sharing information under this duty must also have regard to 
general data sharing principles. Whilst sharing, organisations must be 
satisfied that it is in the interest of the person and incident response to 
share it. They must be satisfied that the information is stored 
appropriately and only used for the purposes in which it is gathered. 
 
3.9 Information Rights 
All individuals whose personal information is held by the Trust have statutory 
rights regarding that information. These are: 
 
3.9.1 The Right to be Informed 
Further information on how the Trust and its staff fulfil this right is detailed 
within the Transparency and Fair Processing section of this policy 
 
3.9.2 The Right of Access 
Commonly known as a Subject Access Request (SAR). Further 
information in this area is described within the Subject Access Request 
section of this policy and the Access to Records Policy.

3.9.3 The Right to Rectification 
The Trust must ensure the accuracy of the personal information it holds. 
However, data subjects also have the right to challenge the accuracy of 
information and request its rectification. 
 
Commonly there will be a business-as-usual process within most 
departments for updating patients records if they are found to be 
incorrect. However more complex or formal requests under this process 
should be referred to the Information Governance Team.  
 
3.9.4 The Right to Erasure 
Under certain circumstances data subjects have the right to request that 
their information be deleted.  
 
This right does not extend to information which is processed as part of 
the Trusts “public task” as an NHS provider for the purposes of health 
care and treatment.  
 
Requests under this process MUST be forwarded to the Information 
Governance Team. 
 
3.9.5 The Right to Restrict Processing 
Under certain circumstances data subjects have the right to request that 
processing of their information be restricted.   
 
Requests under this process will be managed in line with the GDPR and 
regulatory guidance in this area.  
 
Requests under this process MUST be forwarded to the Information 
Governance Team. 
 
3.9.6 The Right to Restrict Processing 
Under certain circumstances data subjects have the right to request 
access to their data in a reasonable form.  
 
Requests made under this right will be managed as per the Trusts 
Subject Access Request process with the support of the Information 
Governance Team.  
 
3.9.7 The Right to Object 
Under certain circumstances data subjects have the right to object to the 
processing of their personal data. 
    
Requests made under this right MUST be forwarded to the Information 
Governance Team.  
 
3.9.8 Rights in relation to automated decision making and profiling 
Data subjects have specific rights regarding the automated individual 
decision-making (making a decision solely by automated means without 
any human involvement) and profiling (automated processing of personal 
data to evaluate certain things about an individual). Profiling can be part 
of an automated decision-making process. 
    
Compliance with these rights will be managed in line with this policy as a 
whole and the Data Protection Principles.
